key_findings.claim: AgentAuditor achieves human-level accuracy in agent safety and security evaluation, matching or exceeding average human expert performance across multiple benchmarks.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Up to 96.3% F1 and 96.1% accuracy on R-Judge with Gemini-2.0-Flash-thinking; human expert average on R-Judge was 95.67% F1 vs AgentAuditor's 96.31% F1
key_findings.context: Evaluated across 8 datasets and 12 LLM backbones; human evaluation conducted with 5 domain experts each having ≥3 months AI safety/security research experience

key_findings.claim: AgentAuditor consistently improves evaluation performance over baseline LLMs across all 8 datasets and all 12 models tested, with no exceptions.
key_findings.quantitative_result: F1 improvements range from +4.1 percentage points (Claude-3.5 on ASSEBench-Safety) to +677.4 percentage points relative gain (Qwen-2.5-7B on AgentHarm); absolute F1 gains up to 38.5 pp on ASSEBench-Security
key_findings.context: Tested on ASSEBench-Security, ASSEBench-Safety, ASSEBench-Strict, ASSEBench-Lenient, R-Judge, AgentHarm, AgentSecurityBench, and AgentSafetyBench

key_findings.claim: FINCH parameter-free hierarchical clustering substantially outperforms K-Means, K-Medoids, and DBSCAN for representative shot selection in reasoning memory construction.
key_findings.quantitative_result: FINCH: 96.31 F1 / 96.10 Acc; K-Means: 88.11 / 86.96; K-Medoids: 89.66 / 86.79; DBSCAN: 85.94 / 84.12 (all on R-Judge with Gemini-2.0-Flash-thinking)
key_findings.context: Ablation conducted on R-Judge; FINCH advantage attributed to automatic hierarchical cluster structure detection without manual hyperparameter tuning

key_findings.claim: Nomic-Embed-Text-v1.5 at 512 dimensions achieves optimal performance-efficiency trade-off among tested embedding models for AgentAuditor's memory system.
key_findings.quantitative_result: 96.31 F1 at 512 dims (522 MB VRAM); Stella-en-1.5B-v5 at 512 dims: 96.46 F1 (5887 MB VRAM, ~10× resources); NV-Embed-v2 at 4096 dims: 91.84 F1 (14975 MB VRAM)
key_findings.context: Embedding dimension is a more critical factor than model size; diminishing returns observed beyond Nomic at 512 dims

key_findings.claim: AgentAuditor is robust to label noise in reasoning memory up to approximately 25% incorrect labels, maintaining performance above the no-memory baseline.
key_findings.quantitative_result: At 25% label noise: F1=0.8536, Acc=0.8333 (vs baseline 0.8227/0.8121); performance falls below baseline at 50% noise. Recall remains above baseline even at 33.3% noise.
key_findings.context: Robustness experiment on R-Judge with Gemini-2.0-Flash-thinking; 24 representative shots used; noise introduced by flipping ground-truth labels

key_findings.claim: AgentAuditor requires only 24 manually annotated records to construct its reasoning memory, compared to 4000 records required for fine-tuning ShieldAgent, while achieving superior performance.
key_findings.quantitative_result: AgentAuditor (QwQ-32B, 24 records): 95.67 F1 / 95.57 Acc; ShieldAgent fine-tuned (Qwen-2.5-7B, 4000 records): 83.67 F1 / 81.38 Acc; Memory construction: 0.12–1.07 GPU hours vs 16 GPU hours for fine-tuning
key_findings.context: Resource comparison on R-Judge benchmark; all models tested on HPC with 4× A100 80G GPUs

key_findings.claim: AgentAuditor demonstrates robust out-of-distribution generalization: cross-domain reasoning memory (constructed from R-Judge, applied to ASSEBench) still significantly improves over baseline.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Cross-domain on ASSEBench-Safety: 86.36 F1 / 86.10 Acc vs baseline 61.79 F1 / 67.82 Acc; in-domain: 91.59 / 90.85. Cross-domain on ASSEBench-Security: 84.55 / 85.12 vs baseline 67.25 / 72.34
key_findings.context: Simulates deployment on new domains before domain-specific memory is available

key_findings.claim: ShieldAgent's reported 91.5% accuracy on AgentSafetyBench is likely overestimated and does not generalize to other benchmarks, suggesting possible overfitting, data leakage, or test set bias.
key_findings.quantitative_result: ShieldAgent achieves only 83.7% F1 on R-Judge, 85.69% Acc on AgentSafetyBench (independent replication), and 76.49%/84.49% Acc on ASSEBench-Lenient/Strict respectively
key_findings.context: Authors confirmed faithful reproduction following original settings; manual sampling review validated ground truth reliability; original test set not publicly accessible for further investigation

key_findings.claim: Structured CoT reasoning traces generated by AgentAuditor exhibit superior alignment with human preferences compared to direct LLM risk descriptions across logical structure, reasoning soundness, and completeness dimensions.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Krippendorff's Alpha = 0.86 (>0.8, indicating good inter-rater agreement); 6 human experts rated 200 CoT traces vs 200 direct risk analyses on 1–5 Likert scale across 3 dimensions
key_findings.context: Human evaluation on 100 cases from ASSEBench-Safety and ASSEBench-Security using Gemini-2.0-Flash-thinking and QwQ-32B

key_findings.claim: AgentAuditor maintains meaningful performance advantage over baseline even under severe white-box adversarial attack where one of three final CoT examples is replaced by a malicious forged CoT.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Level 3 white-box attack (33.3% final CoTs poisoned): 84.65 F1 / 82.72 Acc vs unattacked baseline 82.27 F1 / 81.21 Acc
key_findings.context: Three attack tiers tested: grey-box dataset poisoning, strong grey-box reasoning memory poisoning, white-box final decision attack; all on R-Judge with Gemini-2

key_findings.claim: Agent safety evaluation is more challenging than agent security evaluation because safety failures manifest more subtly and lack explicit malicious signatures, leading to higher dependence on precise LLM-based evaluators.
key_findings.context: Conceptual distinction established to motivate ASSEBench design; safety = unintentional internal failures, security = defense against intentional external manipulation

llm_extraction.methods_summary: AgentAuditor is a three-stage, training-free, memory-augmented reasoning framework. Stage 1 (Feature Memory Construction): a single LLM adaptively extracts structured semantic features (scenario, risk type, behavior mode) from raw agent interaction records and embeds them using Nomic-Embed-Text-v1.5 (512 dims) to form a dual-representation feature memory (human-readable structured data + machine-processable vectors). Stage 2 (Reasoning Memory Construction): embeddings are L2-normalized, weighted, concatenated, and dimensionality-reduced via PCA; FINCH unsupervised hierarchical clustering selects ~10% of dataset size as representative shots; a carefully designed CoT prompt template combined with ground-truth labels is fed to the LLM to generate high-quality chain-of-thought reasoning traces for each representative shot, forming the reasoning memory. Stage 3 (Memory-Augmented Reasoning): for each new query, a two-stage retrieval ranks candidate shots by content-level cosine similarity (Top-n) then re-ranks by weighted feature-level similarity (scenario, risk, behavior) to select the k=3 best CoT examples; these are incorporated into a few-shot CoT prompt for the LLM evaluator to produce a binary safe/unsafe judgment. The same LLM is used throughout all three stages for self-consistency. ASSEBench was constructed via a three-stage human-computer collaborative pipeline: data collection from existing benchmarks (AgentSafetyBench, AgentHarm, AgentSecurityBench, R-Judge), standardization and structured annotation by domain experts with binary labels and metadata, and ambiguous case handling via Strict/Lenient re-labeling. Evaluation used standard binary classification metrics (F1, accuracy, recall, precision) with recall prioritized for safety/security contexts.
llm_extraction.limitations: Binary safe/unsafe classification cannot capture nuanced risk degrees, confidence levels, or differential harm severity across risk types. ASSEBench cannot encompass all emerging or future agent risk scenarios, limiting benchmark completeness. AgentAuditor's performance degrades significantly when >50% of reasoning memory shots carry incorrect labels, establishing a practical noise tolerance threshold. Over-reliance on automated evaluation may foster a false sense of security without complementary safety measures. Cross-domain memory transfer shows meaningful but reduced performance compared to in-domain memory, limiting immediate deployment on entirely novel domains. Insights from the evaluation framework could be exploited by malicious actors to devise evasion strategies. ShieldAgent's performance discrepancy could not be fully investigated due to non-public access to the original test set. Human evaluation involved only 5–6 experts with a minimum 3-month experience threshold, which may not fully represent the diversity of real-world expert judgment. Resource comparison (GPU hours) was performed only on open-source models accessed locally, potentially not reflecting API-based deployment economics.

relationships.description: ASSEBench is presented as a comprehensive successor to R-Judge, the only prior benchmark for LLM-based evaluators in agent safety/security. AgentAuditor is evaluated on R-Judge, where it achieves 96.31 F1 vs R-Judge's baseline evaluator results, substantially improving upon R-Judge's original evaluation methodology.

AgentAuditor's independent replication of ShieldAgent contradicts the claimed 91.5% accuracy on AgentSafetyBench, achieving only ~85.69% Acc under faithful reproduction conditions, suggesting overestimation in the original report due to possible overfitting or test set bias.

ASSEBench incorporates and re-annotates interaction records from AgentSafetyBench, expanding coverage to include security threats and introducing nuanced Strict/Lenient judgment standards absent from AgentSafetyBench.
ASSEBench incorporates and re-annotates records from AgentSecurityBench; AgentAuditor is evaluated against it, demonstrating improvements from 58.14 to 95.09 F1 with Gemini-2.
ToolEmu is cited as a prior agent safety benchmark using rule-based and LLM-based evaluators; AgentAuditor addresses the evaluation limitations demonstrated by such benchmarks.

AgentHarm is incorporated as an evaluation benchmark; AgentAuditor improves GPT-4o evaluation on AgentHarm from 30.26 to 93.55 F1, and human-level comparison shows AgentAuditor approaches expert performance (98.30 vs 99.32 F1).

AgentAuditor adopts the FINCH unsupervised hierarchical clustering algorithm for parameter-free representative shot selection, validating its superiority over K-Means, K-Medoids, and DBSCAN in this new application domain.

Llama-Guard-3 is used as a reference baseline showing that even Meta's extensively fine-tuned safety model struggles with complex agent-level safety judgment (78.7% R-Judge), contextualizing why ShieldAgent's claimed 91.5% accuracy appears implausible and supporting AgentAuditor's motivation.

methodology_details.approach: Training-free memory-augmented RAG framework (AgentAuditor) using LLM-extracted structured semantic features, FINCH clustering for representative shot selection, PCA dimensionality reduction, and multi-stage cosine similarity retrieval to augment LLM-as-a-judge with expert-like chain-of-thought reasoning from experiential memory
datasets: ASSEBench-Safety (1476 records, 9 risk types, 17 scenarios, 14 behavior modes)
ASSEBench-Security (817 records, 6 risk types, 12 scenarios, 12 behavior modes)
metrics: Likert scale ratings (logical structure, reasoning soundness, completeness)
methodology_details.reproducibility_notes: Code and ASSEBench openly accessible at https://github.com/Astarojth/AgentAuditor-ASSEBench. ShieldAgent reproduction code provided. Experiments on HPC with 4× Nvidia Tesla A100 80G GPUs, BF16 precision, vLLM framework. Default hyperparameters: n=10 candidate shots, k=3 final shots, FINCH selecting ~10% of dataset size as representative shots, PCA dimensionality preserving specified cumulative variance proportion. Embedding: Nomic-Embed-Text-v1.5 at 512 dims.

domain_specific_fields.benchmark: ASSEBench (Agent Safety & Security Evaluator Benchmark) — 2293 annotated interaction records, 4 subsets, 15 risk types, 29 application scenarios, 26 agent behavior modes; first benchmark jointly covering LLM agent safety and security evaluation quality
domain_specific_fields.metrics: F1-score (primary), Accuracy, Recall (prioritized for safety-critical contexts), Precision; binary safe/unsafe classification framework; Likert-scale human evaluation (1–5) across logical structure, reasoning soundness, completeness
domain_specific_fields.model_architecture: Three-stage pipeline: (1) LLM-based structured feature extractor (scenario/risk/behavior) → Nomic-Embed-Text-v1.5 encoder → dual feature memory (structured + vectorized); (2) PCA + FINCH clustering → CoT generation via prompted LLM → reasoning memory; (3) Two-stage cosine similarity RAG (content-level Top-n + feature-level re-ranking) → few-shot CoT prompt → LLM judge. Single LLM used consistently across all stages. Tested with Gemini-2.0-Flash-thinking, Claude-3.5, GPT-4o/4.1/o3-mini, DeepSeek-v3, QwQ-32B, Qwen-2.5 series (7B/32B), Llama-3.1-8B.
domain_specific_fields.dataset: ASSEBench: 2293 agent interaction records in JSON format with binary safe/unsafe label, ambiguity flag, scenario, risk type, behavior mode, and risk description. Constructed from reproduced versions of AgentSafetyBench, AgentHarm, AgentSecurityBench, and R-Judge via three-stage human-computer collaborative pipeline. Dual labeling standards (Strict/Lenient) for ambiguous cases. 528 interaction environments across 29 application scenarios.
